items.title: [Sports Science 101 #7] Lift With Your Legs: The Hidden Physics of Every Powerful Move
items.body:
> Great athletes aren't just strong — they're efficient. Biomechanics explains how posture and body position turn muscle force into motion without wasting effort or wrecking your joints.

## Today's Concept

Biomechanics is the study of how forces act on and inside the body when it moves. If last week was about flexibility, this week is about something more fundamental: **where force comes from and how it travels through you**.

Here's the core idea. Almost every powerful human movement — a jump, a throw, a sprint — starts from the ground. You push into the floor, and the floor pushes back with equal force (Newton's third law — this push-back is called the **ground reaction force**). That force then travels up through your body like a wave: feet → legs → hips → torso → shoulders → hands. Scientists call this pathway the **kinetic chain**.

This is why a baseball pitcher's 95 mph fastball isn't really thrown by the arm. Studies of pitching mechanics consistently show that the legs and trunk generate roughly half of the throwing power; the arm mostly *delivers* force created lower down. A pitcher who throws "all arm" is both slower and more likely to get hurt.

Posture matters because it determines how cleanly that force wave travels. A well-aligned body passes force through bones and large muscles. A slouched or twisted body leaks force at every bend — and dumps the leftover stress onto small structures like your lower back, which were never designed to be the engine.

One more tool you need: **torque**. In plain terms:

```
torque = force x distance from the pivot
```

The farther a weight sits from your body, the harder your muscles must work to control it. Double the distance, double the torque. This one equation explains most "good form" rules you've ever heard.

## In Everyday Life

Picture moving day. You've rented a U-Haul, and a friend promised to help in exchange for pizza. Now you're staring at a box of books that weighs about 40 pounds.

**Option A:** You bend at the waist, legs straight, and lift the box with the strength of your lower back — with the box a foot and a half in front of you.

**Option B:** You squat down, pull the box against your chest, and stand up by driving your legs into the ground.

Same box, same 40 pounds. But the physics is wildly different. In Option A, the box sits far from your hips (the pivot point), so the torque on your lower spine is several times the box's actual weight — your back muscles may need to produce hundreds of pounds of force just to keep you from folding forward. In Option B, the load stays close to your body (small distance, small torque), and the force travels up the kinetic chain through your glutes and quads — the biggest, strongest muscles you own.

"Lift with your legs, not your back" isn't gym-teacher folklore. It's the torque equation, applied. The same logic explains why you carry a heavy Costco bag close to your ribs instead of at arm's length, and why snow shoveling injures so many backs every winter: long shovel, load far from the body, huge torque, tired posture.

## 3-Line Recap

- Powerful movement starts with pushing into the ground; force travels up the body through the kinetic chain — the arm delivers what the legs and hips create.
- Good posture is really good *alignment*: it lets force pass through big muscles and bones instead of leaking into vulnerable joints.
- Torque = force x distance. Keeping a load close to your body is the single cheapest way to make any lift safer and easier.

## ✅ Self Quiz

**1. (Multiple choice)** In a baseball pitch, where does most of the throwing power originate?
- (a) The fingers and wrist
- (b) The shoulder and elbow
- (c) The legs and trunk
- (d) Power is split evenly across all joints

**2. (True/False)** Holding a 40-pound box at arm's length puts roughly the same stress on your lower back as holding it against your chest, since the box weighs 40 pounds either way.

**3. (Multiple choice)** The "kinetic chain" refers to:
- (a) A brand of resistance bands
- (b) The sequence by which force travels through linked body segments, usually from the ground up
- (c) The chemical reactions that fuel muscles
- (d) The order of exercises in a workout program

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Biomechanics** — the study of forces acting on and produced by the body during movement.
- **Ground reaction force** — the push the ground gives back when you push into it; the starting point of most athletic power.
- **Kinetic chain** — the linked segments (feet, legs, hips, torso, arms) through which force travels in sequence.
- **Torque** — rotational force; grows with both the size of the load and its distance from the pivot point (like your hips or spine).
- **Center of mass** — the average point where your body's weight is concentrated; keeping loads near it improves balance and efficiency.

---

*Answers: 1 — (c). Research on pitching mechanics shows the legs and trunk generate roughly half of throwing power; the arm mainly transfers and fine-tunes it. 2 — False. Stress on your spine depends on torque, not just weight: the farther the box is from your body, the more force your back muscles must produce to hold it. 3 — (b). The kinetic chain is the ground-up sequence of body segments that passes force from one link to the next.*

items.title: [AFA 2025] The $40 Trillion Blind Spot: Why America's Wealth Gap May Be Smaller Than You Think
items.body:
> An award-winning study finds that once Social Security is counted as household wealth, the widely reported surge in U.S. wealth inequality since 1989 largely disappears.

## What They Presented

At the American Finance Association's annual meeting, the Dimensional Fund Advisors First Prize — which honors top research published in the *Journal of Finance* — went to "Social Security and Trends in Wealth Inequality" by Sylvain Catherine (Wharton), Max Miller (Harvard Business School), and Natasha Sarin (Yale).

Their starting point is simple: the famous statistics showing America's wealth gap exploding count stocks, homes, businesses, and 401(k)s — but leave out Social Security entirely. That's a strange omission, because for most Americans, the promise of a monthly Social Security check for life is one of their most valuable financial assets. It works much like a government-backed pension, yet because it's "pay-as-you-go" (today's workers fund today's retirees), it never shows up on anyone's balance sheet.

The authors fix this. Using household data from the Survey of Consumer Finances, they estimate each family's future Social Security benefits, subtract the payroll taxes they'll still pay, and convert that stream of future money into today's dollars using Treasury bond yields.

The results are striking:

- Social Security wealth grew from $7.2 trillion in 1989 to $40.6 trillion in 2019.
- It now makes up nearly 50% of all wealth held by the bottom 90% of households.
- Once it's included, top wealth shares have changed little over three decades. By the authors' estimates, the rise in the top 1%'s share shrinks from about 6.4 percentage points to roughly 1.5.

The team stress-tested the finding: adjusting for economic risk in future wage growth, modeling a scenario where benefits are cut 40% due to the program's funding shortfall, and even applying an extra discount because Social Security can't be sold or borrowed against. The core conclusion held up.

## Why It Matters

Debates about wealth taxes, retirement policy, and "runaway inequality" all rest on how wealth is measured. This paper doesn't claim inequality is low — the rich still hold far more than everyone else, and income inequality is a separate question. What it shows is that the *trend* looks very different when the biggest asset of ordinary households is actually counted. That matters for anyone designing, debating, or voting on economic policy.

There's a personal-finance angle, too. If you're mid-career and your investment account looks thin, standard net-worth math is understating your position: your future Social Security benefits are a real, bond-like asset — for many households, the largest one they own. Financial planners increasingly treat it that way when building retirement portfolios.

Two honest caveats from the authors: the study covers only retirement wealth (Medicare and Medicaid, which are comparably large, are left for future work), and Social Security is illiquid — you can't sell it, and you can't pass it to your kids.

## The Simple Way to Get It

Imagine comparing two colleagues' retirement readiness. One has a 401(k) worth $500,000. The other has no investment account but a company pension paying a solid check every month for life. If you only count account balances, the second person looks broke — even though the pension may be worth just as much as the 401(k). Social Security is that invisible pension for most American families. This paper simply puts it on the books, and once it's there, the gap between the top and everyone else stops looking like it's spiraling.

## 3-Line Recap

1. Standard wealth-inequality statistics exclude Social Security, the largest asset of most American households.
2. Valued properly, Social Security wealth reached $40.6 trillion by 2019 — nearly half the wealth of the bottom 90% — and top wealth shares have barely risen since 1989 once it's included.
3. The finding, published in the *Journal of Finance* and awarded the AFA's Dimensional Fund Advisors First Prize, reshapes debates on inequality, wealth taxes, and how you should tally your own net worth.

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Social Security wealth**: The value today of all the Social Security benefits a household expects to receive, minus the payroll taxes it will still pay.
- **Present value (discounting)**: Translating money you'll receive in the future into what it's worth today, since a dollar later is worth less than a dollar now.
- **Top wealth share**: The percentage of a country's total wealth held by its richest households, such as the top 1%.
- **Pay-as-you-go system**: A pension design where current workers' taxes directly fund current retirees' benefits, rather than building up a personal account.
- **Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF)**: A detailed Federal Reserve survey of U.S. household assets, debts, and income used in much of wealth-inequality research.
